chest-pain-causes-and-when-to-get-help.name: Chest pain: causes and when to get help
chest-pain-causes-and-when-to-get-help.summary: Most chest pain does not come from the heart, but sudden pain that does not ease or spreads to the arm, jaw, neck or back needs a 999 call.
keyPoints: The NHS says that in most cases chest pain is not caused by a heart problem.
The NHS says to call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not ease, or pain that spreads to the arm, jaw, neck or back.
The NHS says a person with these symptoms should not drive themselves to A&E.

For sharp or stabbing chest pain that gets worse with deep breathing, swallowing, coughing or lying down, as can happen with pericarditis, the NHS pericarditis page suggests an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111.

body.heading: What causes chest pain?
body.body: The NHS says that in most cases chest pain is not caused by a heart problem. Common causes that do not involve the heart include heartburn or indigestion, a strained chest muscle, anxiety or panic, and chest infections such as pneumonia or pleurisy. Shingles can also cause chest pain, often with a skin rash. Angina, heart attack and pericarditis are heart conditions that can cause chest pain. Pericarditis is inflammation of the lining around the heart, and the NHS says it often follows a viral infection such as a cold or flu.

body.heading: How do angina and a heart attack differ?
body.body: Angina is chest pain that is a sign of a heart problem, and GTN can be used to ease an attack or before a known trigger such as exercise. Angina attacks usually last less than 10 minutes. The NHS says chest pain is the most common symptom of a heart attack, but symptoms vary from person to person. Other signs include pain spreading to the arms, jaw, neck or back, sweating, breathlessness and feeling or being sick, and some people have these without any chest pain. Unlike the pain of angina, the symptoms of a heart attack are not usually relieved by a nitrate tablet or spray. A heart attack can be life-threatening and needs emergency treatment in hospital.

body.heading: When is chest pain an emergency?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not ease, or pain that spreads to the arm, jaw, neck or back. Chest pain that comes with sweating, nausea, light-headedness or breathlessness is in the same group. The NHS says a person with these symptoms should not drive themselves to A&E. For someone already diagnosed with angina, the NHS treats pain that does not settle after rest or after their usual angina medicine as an emergency that needs a 999 call.

body.heading: When should chest pain be checked the same day?
body.body: For sharp or stabbing chest pain that gets worse with deep breathing, swallowing, coughing or lying down, as can happen with pericarditis, the NHS pericarditis page suggests an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111. Angina that feels worse than before, happens more often, lasts longer or happens at rest is a reason to contact a GP urgently.

body.heading: What happens at the GP or in hospital?
body.body: If a GP thinks someone may have angina, they can be referred to a heart specialist (cardiologist). Tests to find out whether someone is having a heart attack include an electrocardiogram (ECG) and blood tests, and further tests can include a coronary angiogram. An ECG records the heart's electrical activity. An NHS emergency department leaflet says staff check for serious causes such as a heart attack, a blood clot in the lung and a collapsed lung. The Sussex hospital leaflet says staff may test for troponin, which shows whether the heart is involved, and for D-dimer, which looks for clots in the lungs. The Sussex hospital leaflet says a normal troponin result makes a heart problem less likely, but does not necessarily mean the pain is unrelated to the heart.

body.heading: How are angina and a heart attack treated?
body.body: Tests for a heart attack include an ECG and blood tests, and further tests can include a coronary angiogram, which can show exactly where blood flow to the heart is blocked. A heart attack needs emergency treatment in hospital, and treatment can include medicine, coronary angioplasty (opening blocked arteries with a stent) and coronary artery bypass surgery. NHS treatment for angina aims to help stop attacks and reduce the risk of further problems such as a heart attack. Medicines for angina include GTN, beta blockers, which slow the heart, and calcium channel blockers, which relax the arteries, and surgery may be recommended if medicines are not controlling angina. A GP may ask about lifestyle, such as diet, smoking and drinking, and healthy lifestyle changes alongside treatment can help control angina.

headache-types-causes-and-warning-signs.name: Headaches: types, causes and warning signs
headache-types-causes-and-warning-signs.summary: Tension-type headache is the most common type, and a headache that starts suddenly and is very severe needs a 999 call.
keyPoints: The NHS says the main symptom of a tension headache is pain on both sides of the head, face or neck, which lasts at least 30 minutes and can last much longer.
The NHS describes migraine as a throbbing headache that can be severe, is often on one side of the head and can be worse when moving around.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a headache that comes on suddenly and is extremely painful, or one that follows a serious head injury.
Great Ormond Street Hospital describes medication overuse headache as a headache that develops and gets worse with frequent use of medicines taken for pain.

body.heading: What are the common types of headache?
body.body:
The NHS says the main symptom of a tension headache is pain on both sides of the head, face or neck, which lasts at least 30 minutes and can last much longer. NHS Cheshire and Merseyside describes tension-type headache as the most common headache, usually mild to moderately severe, with a pressing or tightening feel. The NHS says stress is a common cause of tension headaches.

The NHS describes migraine as a throbbing headache that can be severe, is often on one side of the head and can be worse when moving around. Other migraine symptoms include feeling sick and sensitivity to light and sound.

Some people also get an aura, such as seeing zigzag lines or flashing lights. NHS inform says migraine affects around 1 in 5 women and 1 in 15 men. NHS inform describes cluster headaches as rare, coming in bouts of short daily headaches that last a month or two, with pain usually around the eye.

body.heading: Can painkillers cause headaches?
body.body: Great Ormond Street Hospital describes medication overuse headache as a headache that develops and gets worse with frequent use of medicines taken for pain. Great Ormond Street Hospital says medication overuse headache occurs in people who already have tension-type headache or migraine. A Nottinghamshire NHS pathway says headache from overusing painkillers improves or resolves within 3 months of stopping them.

body.heading: Which headaches need a 999 call?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a headache that comes on suddenly and is extremely painful, or one that follows a serious head injury. NHS inform lists other reasons to call 999 or go to A&E, including signs of stroke such as weakness on one side or slurred speech, signs of meningitis or sepsis, and being drowsy or confused.

body.heading: Which headaches need an urgent GP visit?
body.body: NHS inform lists a headache set off by coughing, sneezing, a change in posture or effort as a reason to contact the GP practice urgently, or phone NHS 111 if it is closed. A headache that wakes someone from sleep, or keeps getting worse despite treatment, is listed under contacting the GP practice. NHS inform lists a sore scalp or jaw pain when chewing in someone over 50 as a reason to contact the GP practice urgently, or phone NHS 111 if it is closed. NHS inform lists changes in vision, or a new or worsening headache with dizziness, vomiting or weakness, as reasons to contact the GP practice urgently, or phone NHS 111 if it is closed. An NHS formulary guideline describes giant cell arteritis, also called temporal arteritis, as a medical emergency that needs prompt assessment and immediate steroid treatment to prevent permanent loss of vision.

body.heading: How is migraine treated?
body.body: The NHS describes triptans as a painkiller made specifically for migraine, available as tablets, injections and nasal sprays. NHS inform says a GP may recommend a triptan if over-the-counter medicines are not helping. Anti-sickness medicines can help during a migraine even without nausea, and the NHS says they work better when taken as soon as symptoms begin. The NHS lists stress, tiredness, skipping meals and too much caffeine among common migraine triggers.

body.heading: When is a routine GP visit sensible, and what might the GP do?
body.body: The NHS says tension headaches can be treated with painkillers, but advises seeing a GP for several headaches a week or severe ones. A GP may suggest keeping a migraine diary. There is no specific test for migraine, so the GP looks for a pattern of recurring headaches with the typical symptoms. The NHS says an antidepressant medicine called amitriptyline is sometimes recommended to help prevent tension headaches.

shortness-of-breath-causes-and-next-step.name: Shortness of breath: causes and next steps
shortness-of-breath-causes-and-next-step.summary: Breathlessness has many causes, from asthma and infections to heart and lung disease, and severe difficulty breathing needs a 999 call.
keyPoints: NHS inform lists asthma attacks, pneumonia and heart failure among the likely causes of sudden breathlessness.
Sudden breathlessness could be an asthma attack, which makes it difficult to move air in and out of the airways.
NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for severe difficulty breathing, such as being unable to speak without pausing for breath.
The NHS says to contact NHS 111 for difficulty breathing, feeling or being sick, coughing up blood, or pain or swelling in one leg.

body.heading: Why do people get short of breath?
body.body:
NHS inform lists asthma attacks, pneumonia and heart failure among the likely causes of sudden breathlessness. NHS inform also lists a severe allergic reaction, a collapsed lung and a blood clot in the lung as possible causes of sudden breathlessness. A collapsed lung, or pneumothorax, is a partial collapse of the lung caused by a small tear in the lung surface.

The NHS lists several possible causes of breathlessness, including COPD, scarring of the lungs, heart failure, asthma, chest infections and being overweight. In heart failure, fluid builds up in the lungs and makes breathing harder.

body.heading: What do asthma, COPD, heart failure and a lung clot look like?
body.body: Sudden breathlessness could be an asthma attack, which makes it difficult to move air in and out of the airways. The NHS lists breathlessness as the most common symptom of heart failure; it may happen after activity or at rest, may be worse when lying down, and may wake a person at night. It lists tiredness, swollen ankles and legs, and feeling lightheaded or fainting as other heart failure symptoms. An NHS trust leaflet says the most common symptom of a pulmonary embolism is breathlessness, with chest pain that is worse on breathing or coughing, and it also lists cough and fever.

body.heading: When is breathlessness an emergency?
body.body: NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for severe difficulty breathing, such as being unable to speak without pausing for breath. The NHS says chest tightness or heaviness, or pain that spreads to the arms, back, neck or jaw, is also a reason to call 999 or go to A&E. The NHS adds sudden confusion, or lips or skin turning pale, blue or grey, to the signs for calling 999 or going to A&E. NHS 111 Wales advises that a person should not drive themselves to A&E but should ask someone to take them or call an ambulance.

body.heading: When should breathlessness be seen urgently or soon?
body.body: The NHS says to contact NHS 111 for difficulty breathing, feeling or being sick, coughing up blood, or pain or swelling in one leg. NHS inform advises contacting the GP practice if breathlessness is new or unexplained. The NHS advises seeing a GP if breathlessness has lasted longer than a month, gets worse with normal activity or when lying down, or comes with swollen ankles.

body.heading: What does the GP ask about and test?
body.body: NHS inform's guidance asks whether breathlessness came on suddenly or slowly and whether anything triggered it, such as exercise. An NHS England pathway for persistent breathlessness lists an ECG, a chest X-ray and spirometry among the first-line tests. Spirometry is a breathing test that measures how much air a person can blow out and how fast. The same pathway says an ECG showing atrial fibrillation with breathlessness should prompt a heart specialist assessment, including an echocardiogram.

body.heading: How is breathlessness treated?
body.body: Treatment depends on the cause. For COPD, treatment usually involves relieving symptoms with medicines such as inhalers, and pulmonary rehabilitation may help. Heart failure is managed with lifestyle changes and medicines or surgery. A blood clot in the lung can be treated with anticoagulants, which are drugs that thin the blood. NHS leaflets describe pursed-lip breathing as a technique that can help keep the airways open for longer and reduce the work of breathing, for example in COPD.

stomach-ache-causes-by-area-and-warning-.name: Stomach ache: causes by area and warning signs
stomach-ache-causes-by-area-and-warning-.summary: Where a stomach ache sits helps point to causes such as appendicitis, gallstones or IBS, and sudden severe pain needs 999 or A&E.
keyPoints: The NHS lists trapped wind, indigestion, constipation and a stomach bug or food poisoning as common everyday causes of stomach ache.
The NHS stomach ache page links pain in the lower right side of the tummy with appendicitis.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if the pain started suddenly and is severe.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if the ache suddenly gets much worse, if the person is pregnant, if there is blood in the poo, or if diarrhoea or vomiting has lasted several days.

body.heading: What usually causes a stomach ache?
body.body: The NHS lists trapped wind, indigestion, constipation and a stomach bug or food poisoning as common everyday causes of stomach ache. The NHS links intense pain around the time of a period, sometimes with pain during or after sex and when pooing, with endometriosis.

body.heading: Does the area of the pain point to a cause?
body.body:
The NHS stomach ache page links pain in the lower right side of the tummy with appendicitis. NHS 111 Wales links severe pain that lasts for hours in the upper centre of the tummy, or just under the ribs on the right, with gallstones. It links ongoing cramps, bloating, diarrhoea and constipation with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

NHS inform describes appendicitis as painful swelling of the appendix, and says the pain and cramping of IBS may be relieved by going to the toilet. Stomach ulcer pain is usually in the upper tummy, may feel burning and is often worse at night. Gastritis can cause pain, indigestion and feeling sick. Gastritis is inflammation of the lining of the stomach. Acute pancreatitis causes severe pain around the top of the tummy that develops suddenly, and gallstones and alcohol are its most common causes.

body.heading: What do appendicitis, gallstones and diverticular disease look like?
body.body: Appendicitis is when the appendix becomes inflamed; it usually causes pain in the lower right side of the tummy and is sometimes accompanied by nausea and loss of appetite. An NHS 111 Wales page says appendicitis needs urgent treatment in hospital. Many people with gallstones have no symptoms, but a stone can cause pain, jaundice or pancreatitis. NHS inform says diverticulitis, the inflamed form of diverticular disease, tends to cause more severe tummy pain, especially on the left side, and a fever. NHS 111 Wales advises urgent help from a GP or NHS 111 for blood or mucus in the stool, pain that gets worse or does not go away, or a high temperature or shivers.

body.heading: When is stomach pain an emergency?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if the pain started suddenly and is severe. Other reasons on the NHS page include struggling to breathe, confusion, and blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin, lips or tongue. NHS inform adds chest pain and difficulty breathing to the reasons to call 999. For acute pancreatitis, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden, severe tummy pain together with any of: pain spreading to the back, bloating that does not go away, a fast heartbeat or difficulty breathing.

body.heading: When should it be checked the same day or by a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if the ache suddenly gets much worse, if the person is pregnant, if there is blood in the poo, or if diarrhoea or vomiting has lasted several days.

body.heading: What might a GP do?
body.body: Treatment depends on the cause. For gastritis, a GP might arrange a breath test for Helicobacter pylori bacteria, a stool test or a blood test. Stomach ulcers may be treated with antibiotics for a Helicobacter pylori infection or with medicines that reduce stomach acid, such as proton pump inhibitors.

references.title: NHS inform: Stomach ache and abdominal pain

back-pain-what-helps-and-when-to-get-hel.name: Back pain: what helps and when to get help
back-pain-what-helps-and-when-to-get-hel.summary: Most back pain settles with time and staying active helps, but new numbness around the genitals or changes in bladder or bowel control need urgent help, and NHS leaflets point to A&E or NHS 111.
keyPoints: NHS sources say that staying active is part of treatment and that most back pain settles with time.
NICE guideline NG59 on low back pain and sciatica in people over 16 recommends considering a group exercise programme for a specific episode or flare-up.
NHS sources suggest asking a GP or an NHS physiotherapist for advice if back symptoms are still getting in the way of normal activities after about 6 weeks.
Cauda equina syndrome is a rare but serious condition that needs emergency treatment.

body.heading: What causes back pain?
body.body: An NHS back pain page says a strain is a common cause and that serious causes such as a fracture, cancer or infection are very rare. The NHS says a slipped disc is the most common cause of sciatica, and the likelihood rises with age. Other causes of sciatica include spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis and a back injury. Sciatica is pain that spreads from the lower back down the leg because the sciatic nerve is irritated.

body.heading: What helps back pain?
body.body: NHS sources say that staying active is part of treatment and that most back pain settles with time. NHS inform describes keeping active as an essential part of treatment and recovery. In most cases, back pain gets better after a few weeks. NHS inform says resting in bed does not help back pain and often makes it harder to get going again. The NHS sciatica page suggests asking a pharmacist about painkillers and says paracetamol is unlikely to help sciatica. The NHS back pain page says paracetamol on its own is not recommended for back pain.

body.heading: What does NICE recommend for low back pain?
body.body: NICE guideline NG59 on low back pain and sciatica in people over 16 recommends considering a group exercise programme for a specific episode or flare-up. NICE guideline NG59 says not to offer belts or corsets, foot supports, traction or TENS for low back pain.

body.heading: When should back pain be seen by a GP or physiotherapist?
body.body: NHS sources suggest asking a GP or an NHS physiotherapist for advice if back symptoms are still getting in the way of normal activities after about 6 weeks. NHS 111 Wales says physiotherapy is free on the NHS and that, depending on where a person lives, they may be able to refer themselves or may need to see a GP first. Sciatica often improves within weeks, though it can last longer.

body.heading: What are the emergency signs?
body.body: Cauda equina syndrome is a rare but serious condition that needs emergency treatment. NHS sources list its warning signs as changes in bladder or bowel control, numbness or pins and needles around the genitals or back passage, and pain or weakness in both legs. One NHS trust leaflet says to attend the Emergency Department immediately if two or more of these symptoms appear suddenly, and another says to attend A&E or call NHS 111.

references.title: NICE NG59: Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s

knee-pain-causes-self-care-and-when-to-a.name: Knee pain: causes and when to get help
knee-pain-causes-self-care-and-when-to-a.summary: Knee pain can often be treated at home, and NHS 111 is the route for a badly swollen knee or a hot, red knee with a high temperature.
keyPoints: The NHS knee pain page lists causes including sprains and strains, tendonitis, torn ligaments, tendons or meniscus, a dislocated kneecap, bursitis, gout and Osgood-Schlatter's disease.
The NHS says knee pain can often be treated at home by reducing weight on the knee, using an ice pack and taking painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen.
Hampshire and Isle of Wight NHS guidance suggests seeing a GP if knee pain has not eased within a few weeks.
The NHS advises calling NHS 111 if the knee is badly swollen or has changed shape, or if there is a very high temperature with redness or heat around the knee, which can signal infection.

body.heading: What causes knee pain?
body.body: The NHS knee pain page lists causes including sprains and strains, tendonitis, torn ligaments, tendons or meniscus, a dislocated kneecap, bursitis, gout and Osgood-Schlatter's disease. The NHS knee pain page links sprains and strains to overstretching, overusing or twisting the knee, often during exercise. An NHS trust leaflet lists pain, stiffness after rest and swelling as symptoms of osteoarthritis. NHS inform says the exact cause of knee osteoarthritis is unclear, and risk factors include ageing, a previous knee injury, being overweight and family history. An NHS trust page says changes seen on an X-ray do not necessarily match how bad the symptoms are. NHS inform says strengthening the muscles around the knee helps manage osteoarthritis symptoms.

body.heading: What can ease it at home?
body.body: The NHS says knee pain can often be treated at home by reducing weight on the knee, using an ice pack and taking painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen.

body.heading: When should knee pain be seen by a GP or physiotherapist?
body.body: Hampshire and Isle of Wight NHS guidance suggests seeing a GP if knee pain has not eased within a few weeks. The NHS says people may be able to refer themselves to community musculoskeletal (MSK) physiotherapy services without seeing a GP. An NHS trust leaflet describes physiotherapy as the mainstay of treatment for pain at the front of the knee. An NHS trust leaflet on hip and knee osteoarthritis describes regular exercise, over-the-counter pain relief and losing a small amount of body fat.

body.heading: Which signs need urgent help?
body.body: The NHS advises calling NHS 111 if the knee is badly swollen or has changed shape, or if there is a very high temperature with redness or heat around the knee, which can signal infection.

references.title: www.newcastle-hospitals.nhs.uk: osteoarthritis oa hip and knee
www.sfh-tr.nhs.uk: pil202510 05 akpct anterior knee pain causes and treatments.pdf

joint-pain-causes-and-when-to-see-a-gp.name: Joint pain: causes and when to see a GP
joint-pain-causes-and-when-to-see-a-gp.summary: Joint pain has many causes, including osteoarthritis, injury and gout, and the NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for a hot, swollen joint with a fever.
keyPoints: The NHS says to rest the joint but not stop moving it altogether, and that a pharmacist or GP can advise about painkillers.
The NHS suggests a GP appointment if joint pain stops normal activities or affects sleep, keeps getting worse or coming back, or has not improved after 2 weeks of treating it at home.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for severe pain and swelling in one joint that started suddenly.

body.heading: What causes joint pain?
body.body: Gout is a form of arthritis in which small crystals form inside and around the joints. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system targets the joints, with stiffness that is often worse in the morning or after a period of inactivity. The NHS says rheumatoid arthritis is usually first felt in the small joints of the hands and feet. The NHS arthritis overview says gout often affects the big toe joint, which can become painful, swollen and hot. Psoriatic arthritis causes joint pain, stiffness and swelling, and is linked with the skin condition psoriasis, which causes a red, scaly rash.

body.heading: What can ease joint pain at home?
body.body: The NHS says to rest the joint but not stop moving it altogether, and that a pharmacist or GP can advise about painkillers. NHS 111 Wales says being overweight often makes osteoarthritis worse, because it puts extra strain on some joints. NHS 111 Wales describes exercise as one of the most important treatments for osteoarthritis, and says hot or cold packs can relieve symptoms in some people. NHS 111 Wales says osteoarthritis has no cure but does not necessarily get worse over time.

body.heading: When is a GP appointment sensible?
body.body: The NHS suggests a GP appointment if joint pain stops normal activities or affects sleep, keeps getting worse or coming back, or has not improved after 2 weeks of treating it at home. It also lists joints that stay stiff for more than 30 minutes after waking. For gout, the NHS advises seeing a GP for a first episode, or when the usual treatments are not helping.

body.heading: Which joint pain needs urgent help?
body.body: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for severe pain and swelling in one joint that started suddenly. A warm, swollen joint that is hard to move, with a high temperature or feeling hot and shivery, may mean a joint infection called septic arthritis.

body.heading: How is the cause found?
body.body: A GP examines the joints for swelling, checks how easily they move and asks about symptoms. Blood tests such as ESR, CRP and a full blood count may be used, and X-rays or MRI scans may show inflammation and damage. No blood test can definitively prove or rule out rheumatoid arthritis, although several tests can show signs of it. If rheumatoid arthritis is suspected, the GP usually refers the person to a rheumatologist. A rheumatologist is a doctor who specialises in conditions of the joints and immune system.

feeling-sick-and-vomiting-in-adults.name: Feeling sick and vomiting in adults
feeling-sick-and-vomiting-in-adults.summary: NHS inform says vomiting in adults usually lasts only 1 or 2 days, but blood in vomit means calling 999 or going to A&E, and vomiting for more than 2 days is a reason to call NHS 111.
keyPoints: The NHS says feeling sick is common and usually goes away on its own.
NHS inform lists signs of severe dehydration, including confusion, a rapid heartbeat, sunken eyes and passing little or no urine, among the reasons to call NHS 111.
NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for vomit that contains blood or looks like coffee granules, or for green or yellow-green vomit.
The NHS advises seeing a GP if the sickness has not improved after a few days or keeps coming back, and calling NHS 111 for advice if a GP cannot be seen.

body.heading: What causes nausea and vomiting?
body.body: The NHS says feeling sick is common and usually goes away on its own. Diarrhoea or vomiting can point to norovirus or food poisoning, and a headache with a high temperature can suggest an infection such as flu. Other causes include morning sickness in pregnancy, motion sickness, anxiety, alcohol, medicines and recent surgery. NHS inform calls gastroenteritis one of the most common causes of vomiting in adults, and also lists migraine, labyrinthitis, appendicitis and medicines such as antibiotics and opioid painkillers. NHS inform says norovirus usually clears up by itself within a few days, and that there is no specific treatment, so the illness has to run its course. NHS inform says antibiotics will not help norovirus because it is caused by a virus, and that small sips of water help to prevent dehydration.

body.heading: What can help at home?
body.body: The NHS describes getting fresh air, sipping cold drinks, trying ginger or peppermint tea, and eating smaller, more frequent meals. It also lists hot, fried or greasy food, eating too quickly and lying down soon after eating as things to avoid. NHS inform advises resting at home and taking small sips of water or squash often so that dehydration does not develop.

body.heading: What are the signs of dehydration?
body.body: NHS inform lists signs of severe dehydration, including confusion, a rapid heartbeat, sunken eyes and passing little or no urine, among the reasons to call NHS 111. NHS inform advises people with diabetes who have been vomiting a lot to call NHS 111, especially if they take insulin, because vomiting can affect blood sugar levels.

body.heading: Which symptoms need urgent help?
body.body: NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for vomit that contains blood or looks like coffee granules, or for green or yellow-green vomit. NHS inform advises calling NHS 111 for a person who keeps being sick and cannot keep fluids down, has been vomiting for more than 2 days, or has lost a lot of weight since becoming ill; its gastroenteritis page lists fever and bloody diarrhoea as reasons to contact NHS 111 or the GP practice urgently. The NHS says to call 999 if sudden sickness comes with tight or heavy chest pain, pain spreading to the arms, back, neck or jaw, or shortness of breath, because these could be signs of a heart attack.

body.heading: When should a GP be involved?
body.body: The NHS advises seeing a GP if the sickness has not improved after a few days or keeps coming back, and calling NHS 111 for advice if a GP cannot be seen. The GP can look for the cause and may prescribe anti-sickness medicine. The NHS says a pregnant person who is being sick often and cannot keep food down should tell their midwife or doctor, or contact the hospital, as soon as possible.

persistent-cough-causes-tests-and-when-t.name: A cough that will not go: causes and tests
persistent-cough-causes-tests-and-when-t.summary: The NHS advises a GP visit for a cough lasting over 3 weeks, and an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for coughing up blood.
keyPoints: The NHS advises seeing a GP if a cough has lasted more than 3 weeks, if weight is being lost for no reason, or if the immune system is weakened.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for a cough with chest pain or a feeling of being very unwell.

The NHS cough page advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for coughing up blood or finding it hard to breathe, and the NHS bronchitis page says to call 999 if someone is struggling to breathe, for example choking or gasping and unable to speak.
The NHS says most coughs can be managed at home with rest and fluids, and a pharmacist can advise on cough medicines.

body.heading: What causes a cough that lasts?
body.body: The NHS cough page lists smoking, heartburn (acid reflux), allergies and infections such as bronchitis as causes. NHS guidance describes asthma, bronchiectasis, acid reflux and postnasal drip as causes of a long-lasting cough. Some NHS hospital trust leaflets list ACE inhibitors, a type of blood pressure medicine, as a cause of a long-lasting cough. NHS inform says a persistent cough is often of unknown cause. The NHS says bronchitis often gets better without treatment in around 3 weeks. A chest infection usually gets better on its own in about 7 to 10 days, although the cough and mucus can last up to 3 weeks. Antibiotics are generally not used for viral chest infections such as flu or viral bronchitis.

body.heading: What can help at home?
body.body: The NHS says most coughs can be managed at home with rest and fluids, and a pharmacist can advise on cough medicines. A local NHS self-care leaflet says there is little evidence on whether over-the-counter cough medicines relieve symptoms.

body.heading: When should a cough be seen by a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises seeing a GP if a cough has lasted more than 3 weeks, if weight is being lost for no reason, or if the immune system is weakened. A South East London Cancer Alliance page urges people with a persistent cough to contact their GP. The NHS lung cancer symptoms page lists symptoms including chest or shoulder pain, weight loss without trying, and tiredness.

body.heading: When is a cough urgent?
body.body: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for a cough with chest pain or a feeling of being very unwell. The NHS cough page advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for coughing up blood or finding it hard to breathe, and the NHS bronchitis page says to call 999 if someone is struggling to breathe, for example choking or gasping and unable to speak. For people with bronchiectasis, the NHS says to call 999 if more than a few streaks of blood are coughed up.

body.heading: What does the GP do?
body.body: A GP may listen to the chest. NHS inform says a GP may arrange tests such as a chest X-ray, breathing or lung function tests, and a sample of phlegm. NHS pages say antibiotics are not usually prescribed for coughs, and a GP may refer people to a specialist if the cause is unclear.

sore-throat-causes-treatment-and-when-to.name: Sore throat: causes, treatment, when to act
sore-throat-causes-treatment-and-when-to.summary: Most sore throats are caused by viruses and clear up on their own, but struggling to breathe or swallow needs 999 or A&E.
keyPoints: NICE says acute sore throat is often caused by a viral infection, and most people get better without an antibiotic.
A sore throat usually clears up on its own and often lasts about a week.
NICE says most people with a sore throat will not need an antibiotic.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for difficulty breathing, being unable to swallow, or drooling.

body.heading: What causes a sore throat?
body.body: NICE says acute sore throat is often caused by a viral infection, and most people get better without an antibiotic. A University Hospitals Sussex NHS leaflet lists tonsillitis, laryngitis, strep throat and glandular fever as other common causes of a sore throat. NICE suggests scoring tools (FeverPAIN or Centor) to spot people with a sore throat who may be more likely to benefit from an antibiotic, and these include fever, pus on the tonsils, tender neck glands and no cough.

body.heading: How long does it last, and what helps?
body.body: A sore throat usually clears up on its own and often lasts about a week. NHS 111 Wales says a pharmacist can advise about paracetamol or ibuprofen for the pain, and a hospital trust leaflet notes that not everyone can take ibuprofen safely.

body.heading: Are antibiotics needed?
body.body: NICE says most people with a sore throat will not need an antibiotic. NICE says a scoring tool (FeverPAIN or Centor) should be used to identify people with a sore throat who may be more likely to benefit from an antibiotic.

body.heading: What are tonsillitis, glandular fever and quinsy?
body.body: A GP can often diagnose tonsillitis from the symptoms and a look at the throat, a swab can show whether bacteria are the cause, and a blood test for glandular fever is recommended if symptoms are severe or will not go away. The NHS says glandular fever is most common in people aged 15 to 24. Antibiotics do not work for glandular fever because it is caused by a virus. Quinsy is a collection of pus between the tonsil and the wall of the throat, and is a complication of tonsillitis.

body.heading: When should a GP be seen?
body.body: The NHS says to contact a GP practice if a sore throat has not started to improve after a week, and to ask for an urgent GP appointment or call NHS 111 for a very high temperature, feeling hot, cold or shivery, or a weakened immune system. A sore throat that does not get better within 10 to 14 days, or that gets worse rather than better, may suggest glandular fever.

body.heading: When is a sore throat an emergency?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for difficulty breathing, being unable to swallow, or drooling. Other reasons are a high-pitched noise when breathing in, a sore throat that is severe and getting worse quickly, swelling inside the mouth or throat, or trouble speaking. NHS 111 Wales advises that a person should not drive themselves to A&E but should ask someone to drive them or call 999.
